strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: missing folklore lemmas in Mathlib cause last-mile formalization friction, and the proactive mining framing is valuable.

The four-agent pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover) is clearly described with algorithm, prompt templates, and runtime configurations, making the engineering approach transparent and partially reproducible.
Produces large-scale artifacts: 4,028 type-checked statements and 1,812 verified proofs, with a few lemmas reportedly merged into Mathlib, indicating real-world utility beyond a toy benchmark.

The human provability audit and failure-mode analysis provide useful insight into remaining errors (e.g., missing hypotheses dominate), and the model evaluation reports interesting findings about specialist vs. generalist provers and ensemble diversity.
weaknesses: The benchmark's validity is not established: the audit finds only 78% of sampled model-unsolved residuals are human-provable, with the remainder including formally false statements due to missing hypotheses or false conjectures. The paper neither filters these invalid instances nor adjusts evaluation metrics, so reported success rates conflate model failure with unprovable/false benchmark items. The 78% figure is based on only 138 audited instances and is extrapolated without confidence intervals.

There is a circularity/contamination concern: GPT-5.1 is used for discovery, judging, and formalization, and is then evaluated on the resulting benchmark. No control is provided for self-bias, memorization of Mathlib seeds, or training-data leakage, undermining the 'closed-book' reasoning claim.

The methodological novelty is limited: the multi-agent generate-judge-repair-prove pipeline closely resembles prior lemma synthesis and proof-repair systems (e.g., LeanConjecturer, Lemmanaid, Delta Prover, APOLLO). The paper does not provide ablations of its agents or direct experimental comparisons to these baselines, and the 'first' claim is overstated.

Evaluation is weak for an ICML benchmark contribution: only Success@2 is reported, with no Pass@k, error bars, or statistical significance; no comparison to standard proving baselines on the same statements; and no analysis of how invalid statements affect model rankings.

The verified-library claim is ambiguous: 1,812 proofs equals 44.99% of 4,028, matching the union of all evaluated models, yet the text says 'Using the Prover agent' singular. It is unclear whether the library comes from one model or the ensemble, making the artifact's provenance and the main results inconsistent.
Upstreaming evidence is very thin: only 3 lemmas were merged, and details/repository links are omitted. This is weak support for the claim of alignment with expert standards and real-world utility.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code/data link is absent from the manuscript, exact model versions and API settings are not fully specified, and the pipeline depends on proprietary GPT-5.1 and a custom Lean server.

strengths: Motivates an important practical bottleneck: missing 'folklore' lemmas in Mathlib create last-mile friction and degrade LLM formal reasoning, with concrete examples from Tao's PFR project and conditional expectation.
Proposes a clear multi-agent pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover) with prompts, algorithm, and hyperparameters documented in appendices, supporting some reproducibility.
Produces substantial artifacts: 4,028 type-checked Lean statements and 1,812 kernel-checked proofs, with code/data promised for release.
Reports a human audit of 138 model-unsolved residuals in which 78% were human-proved, suggesting many generated statements are not outright hallucinations.
Evaluates a diverse set of models across three domains and highlights model complementarity via union performance (44.99% vs. best individual 22.32%).
Includes a limitations section acknowledging deduplication, semantic drift, and the gap between kernel-checked proofs and mergeable Mathlib contributions.
weaknesses: The benchmark's central validity claim is under-supported: statements are LLM-generated and only type-checked; there is no systematic check that they are novel, non-duplicate, or actually 'folklore' rather than already-present or trivial variants. Deduplication relies only on syntactic uniqueness and an aesop triviality filter.

The Judge runs before the Formalizer, and the Formalizer can alter statements to fix syntax; there is no re-judging or semantic-preservation check. Type-checking with sorry does not ensure the repaired statement has the same mathematical meaning or is true, so semantic drift can silently corrupt benchmark instances.

The human audit is too small and biased to establish overall soundness. It samples only 138 instances from the subset unsolved by all models (2 per seed), lacks confidence intervals/inter-annotator agreement, and uses an open-book, AI-assisted protocol. The 78% figure applies to unsolved residuals, not all 4,028 statements; the manuscript conflates 'human-proved' with 'mathematically sound'.

Evaluation contamination is possible and unaddressed. GPT-5.1 is used for generation, judging, and formalization, and the paper evaluates GPT-5.1 on the resulting benchmark; the Prover model that generated the 1,812 proofs in Section 6 is not specified. If the same model was used, its benchmark scores may be inflated, and in any case the omission prevents reproducibility.

No ablation studies support the claimed necessity of the multi-agent design. The paper argues that factorizing failure modes is essential, but does not compare the pipeline against end-to-end generation, or against removing the Judge/Formalizer, so the contribution of each component is unmeasured.

Real-world utility evidence is minimal and unverifiable: only 3 representative lemmas are reported as merged into Mathlib, and code/PR details are omitted for anonymity. This is too little to validate the system's practical impact at the claimed scale.

The evaluation protocol has fairness and reproducibility issues: Success@2 uses only two sequential repair turns; no Pass@k or independent-sample results are reported; some models receive injected imports/options; 'GPT-Reasoning' is only GPT-5.1 with low reasoning, not a full reasoning variant; and model naming is inconsistent (e.g., 'Qwen-200B' vs. Qwen3-235B).

The methodological novelty is limited. The system is a standard LLM judge/formalizer/prover loop; related work (LeanConjecturer, Lemmanaid, Lego-Prover, Delta Prover, etc.) already covers lemma synthesis, library expansion, and feedback-driven repair. The 'first LLM-based multi-agent system for folklore lemmas' claim is overstated without a rigorous comparison.

The benchmark lacks ground-truth proofs and cannot cleanly separate model failure from invalid or unprovable statements except through the small audit. The claimed theoretical solvability of ~88% is derived from that small biased sample and should not be treated as a reliable upper bound.

The notion of 'folklore' is not formally defined or measured. The Discovery prompt asks for missing obvious lemmas, but there is no quantitative evidence that generated statements correspond to actual folklore gaps rather than arbitrary new lemmas, so the main task claim is not empirically established.

The paper's claims are stronger than the evidence: 'validated', 'rigorous', and 'minimizes hallucination' are not supported by the small audit and three upstreamed lemmas. The conclusion also acknowledges semantic drift and deduplication problems but does not resolve them.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important bottleneck in formal mathematics: the absence of small 'folklore' lemmas that make Lean/Mathlib usable for everyday formalization. The task formulation of automated folklore mining is novel and useful.

The multi-agent pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover) is clearly specified, with kernel-in-the-loop verification, explicit prompts, hyperparameters, and pseudocode. Factorizing semantic filtering, syntactic repair, and proof search is a sensible engineering design.

Produces substantial and verifiable artifacts: 4,028 type-checked Lean statements, 1,812 kernel-checked proofs, and at least 3 lemmas merged into Mathlib. The successful Mathlib merges provide real-world evidence that the pipeline can meet expert standards.

Evaluation spans multiple state-of-the-art models, three mathematical domains, a closed-book protocol, and a human audit of model-unsolved instances. The analysis of specialist vs. generalist models and ensemble diversity is informative.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: prompts, runtime configurations, Lean server setup, artifact organization, and limitations are documented. The paper honestly acknowledges deduplication, semantic drift, and upstreaming gaps.
weaknesses: The benchmark validity claim is overstated. The human audit is only on model-unsolved residuals, not the full benchmark, and the reported 78% is a human-provable rate, not a 'mathematically sound' rate. The audit's own failure analysis shows missing hypotheses (21/31) and false conjectures (3/31), so the benchmark contains false or unprovable statements. The abstract's claim that 78% are mathematically sound and that this 'confirms the framework minimizes hallucination' is not supported.

There is no ablation of the multi-agent design. The paper asserts that factorizing failure modes is essential, but provides no controlled comparison against single-agent generation, a no-Judge variant, a no-Formalizer variant, or existing lemma-generation systems such as LeanConjecturer. Thus the central architectural claim is not empirically validated.

The verified library is ambiguously described. Section 6.1 says 1,812 proofs were synthesized 'using the Prover agent,' but Table 3 reports GPT alone at 19.81% and the union of all evaluated models at 44.99% (=1,812/4,028). It is unclear whether the library is from a single Prover agent or the union of all models, which affects interpretation and reproducibility.

Benchmark quality control is weak. Deduplication relies on syntactic uniqueness and aesop triviality, with semantic duplicates and formalizer-induced semantic drift left unmeasured. The Judge Agent rejects many valid candidates (46% of audited rejections were valid), and using GPT-5.1 for both generation and judging risks correlated bias. The benchmark is also generated by GPT-5.1 and then used to evaluate GPT-5.1, raising potential self-preference concerns.

The human audit has limitations: the sample is small (138), covers only unsolved residuals, and the paper inconsistently describes it as 'LLM-assisted' (abstract) versus 'manual' (Section 4.3). The 'theoretical upper bound' language is incorrect: 78% human-provable among unsolved residuals gives a lower bound on provability, not an upper bound. Confidence intervals and sampling details are not reported.

Reproducibility and fairness are not fully established. The main pipeline uses proprietary GPT-5.1, the code/data URL is omitted in the manuscript, and per-model environment injections (e.g., import Aesop, set_option maxHeartbeats 0) may affect fair comparison. The upstreaming evidence is only 3 lemmas and details are omitted for anonymity, so it remains anecdotal.

Presentation issues remain: model naming is confusing ('GPT' vs. 'GPT-Reasoning' as low reasoning), labels are inconsistent across text and tables (e.g., Qwen-200B vs. Qwen3-235B), and several citations have mismatched years (e.g., Masser 2020 for 1985, Mathlib-Community 2018 for 2020, Liu et al. 2019 for 2025).

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: the last-mile gap caused by missing folklore lemmas in formal libraries, complementing saturated Olympiad-style benchmarks.
Introduces a modular four-stage pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover) with a clear rationale of factorizing semantic, syntactic, and proof-search failure modes.

Uses Lean kernel checking plus a proof-bypass screen rejecting sorry, admit, sorryAx, axiom, constant, and opaque declarations, which strengthens the credibility of the 1,506 reported verified proofs.
Provides external validation through a small Mathlib upstreaming pilot in which 3 of 6 submitted lemmas were merged, showing selected outputs can meet expert curation standards.

Constructs a large benchmark of 4,028 non-trivial type-checked Lean statements with a useful three-domain stratification (Foundational, Applied, Abstract) and a described aesop-based triviality filter.

Reports a seed-stratified residual provability audit (138 instances, 78% human-proved) and a held-out audit (84% human-proved), supporting the claim that many model-unsolved residuals are valid rather than hallucinations.

Evaluates a diverse set of frontier and open-weight provers and surfaces interesting qualitative findings about specialist vs. generalist models, test-time compute, and model diversity/union coverage.
Limitations and impact are discussed honestly, including model-dependent benchmark construction, weak novelty filters, possible semantic drift during repair, version pinning, and curation burden.
weaknesses: The central 'folklore' and 'missingness' claim is not quantitatively validated. Novelty relies mainly on prompting and syntactic uniqueness; there is no systematic semantic equivalence or redundancy check against Mathlib. The 1,506 proofs may contain many restatements of existing facts, and one of the six upstreamed lemmas was rejected as redundant.

No downstream utility experiment is provided. The paper does not show that the generated library helps human formalizers or LLM provers, nor does it measure retrieval-augmented proof success; the practical 'library expansion' impact is therefore asserted rather than demonstrated.

Benchmark validity is incompletely characterized. The human audit samples only model-unsolved residuals, not solved instances or the full benchmark. Since 22% of audited unsolved residuals were invalid, the overall false-statement rate is unknown, and the extrapolated ~86% solvable fraction is diagnostic rather than a precise benchmark-level estimate.

Generation and evaluation are confounded: GPT-5.1 is used for discovery, judging, and statement repair, and GPT-5.1 variants are also evaluated as provers. This may introduce self-preference, style bias, or contamination effects that are not controlled for, making cross-model comparisons less clean.

The Judge module is weakly characterized. The audit of rejected candidates found 46% valid false negatives, but the precision of accepted statements is not audited. Thus the semantic filter may discard many good candidates while still admitting false statements.

The Formalizer can change mathematical meaning, and no semantic-preservation check is performed. The authors acknowledge this, but without measuring semantic drift, type-checked statements may not correspond to the intended folklore lemmas.

Reproducibility is hindered by the manuscript's unavailable artifact link: the code and data availability statement contains no accessible URL or repository identifier. Prompts and configurations are provided, but the actual benchmark and proof artifacts cannot be verified from the submission.

Main experimental results lack statistical rigor. Differences between some models are small, yet no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported; the headline 'Union (All Models)' and '37% proved' aggregate across models and repair rounds rather than representing a single reproducible system.

Evaluation setup may not be fully fair across models. The paper mentions injecting environment configurations such as import Aesop and set_option maxHeartbeats 0 when required by specific models, which can advantage some provers. The anomalously low Goedel-Prover-V2-8B Pass@16 result (0.32%) is not reconciled with the stronger 32B Success@2 result.

The technical novelty is modest: the modules are largely standard LLM generation, LLM-as-judge, and repair loops. The main originality lies in task framing and artifact construction, which is valuable but does not by itself resolve the missing novelty and utility validation.

The triviality/redundancy filter is weak: aesop immediate solvability only detects a narrow form of triviality and does not address semantic redundancy, alternate names, or broader Mathlib coverage. This further undermines the claim that the benchmark targets genuinely missing folklore.

Presentation has minor but noticeable issues: figure/image rendering is poor, appendix code listings appear malformed, and some citations are inconsistent (e.g., Gao et al. 2020 vs. 2025, Hubert et al. 2025 vs. 2026, OpenAI reference ordering).

strengths: Targets a real and practically important bottleneck in Lean/Mathlib: the absence of many routine 'folklore' lemmas that block everyday formalization.
The modular pipeline design is clearly motivated: discovery, semantic judging, syntactic repair, and proof search factorize failure modes in a sensible way.
The paper produces a substantial artifact: 4,028 type-checked statements and 1,506 Lean-checked proofs that pass a proof-bypass screen, which could be useful if properly validated and released.

The authors make a serious attempt at validity auditing, including a 138-instance seed-stratified audit and a 94-instance held-out audit, and they report a failure-mode analysis for unproven residuals.
The selective upstreaming pilot, if verifiable, provides a useful external signal that some generated lemmas can meet Mathlib curation standards.
The appendix documents prompts, runtime configurations, extraction logic, and the proof-bypass screen, showing an intent toward reproducibility.
The paper reports cost estimates and explicitly discusses several limitations, including weak novelty filtering and possible redundancy.
weaknesses: The central 'folklore mining' claim is not adequately supported. The Discovery module is essentially an LLM prompted to generate plausible missing lemmas from a seed file; there is no repository-wide search, dependency-graph traversal, or proof-attempt-driven gap detection to establish that generated statements are actually missing or reusable connective tissue. The authors admit that novelty filters rely mainly on syntactic uniqueness and aesop-triviality, so many outputs may be redundant restatements of existing Mathlib facts.

The benchmark's validity is uncertain. The statements are LLM-generated and have no ground-truth proofs. Only 138 of 4,028 instances were audited in the main residual audit, and 22% of audited residuals remained unproven; among failures, 16% were 'false as stated' and 81% had missing hypotheses. The Judge Module's precision is not measured, and the Formalizer can alter a statement after judging without any semantic-preservation check, so the final benchmark may contain invalid or meaning-shifted instances.

There is a serious evaluation-contamination problem. GPT-5.1 is used for candidate discovery, judging, and statement repair, and then GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.1 reasoning are evaluated on the resulting benchmark. The benchmark distribution is therefore shaped by the same model family being scored, and no held-out generation split or independent benchmark construction is provided. The authors acknowledge generation-model dependence but do not resolve the evaluation bias.

Reproducibility is materially compromised in the provided manuscript. The code/data availability sentence ends with 'available at' and no URL; Table 5 lists blank PR and merge-commit fields for the claimed Mathlib merges. These omissions prevent verification of the central external-validation claim and make the artifact hard to use.

The main experimental protocol is not standard and is under-analyzed. Success@2 sequential repair with compiler feedback is not directly comparable to Pass@k or closed-book proving, and the main results lack multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The Pass@16 result for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B is 0.32% overall, while the 32B variant reports 17.70% Success@2; no 8B Success@2 run is given to isolate scale versus protocol effects.

The provenance of the 1,506 verified library proofs is unclear. The paper does not specify which prover model produced them or how they relate to the evaluated models and benchmark instances. If the same statements were used both to generate the library and to evaluate models, overlap and contamination are not controlled.

The proof-bypass screen is narrow. It rejects sorry/admit/sorryAx and new axiom/constant/opaque declarations, but it does not check for redundancy with Mathlib, semantic preservation, triviality beyond aesop, or proof-style maintainability. Thus the 'verified library' may contain many trivial, duplicate, or non-folklore artifacts.

The human audit is open-book with full Mathlib, AI assistance, and external search, so it does not establish intrinsic validity under the closed-book benchmark protocol; the sample is also drawn from model-unsolved residuals and is not a full benchmark validation.

The presentation contains overclaims and tangential material. The ABC conjecture introduction is largely irrelevant, and claims such as 'first' and 'pioneering' are not supported by a controlled comparison to prior lemma-conjecturing systems like LeanConjecturer or Lemmanaid. The comparison remains qualitative rather than experimental.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: the last-mile barrier in formal mathematics caused by missing folklore lemmas in Mathlib.
Introduces a novel task formulation, automated folklore mining, and a modular pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover) that factorizes distinct failure modes.
Produces substantial artifacts: 4,028 non-trivial type-checked Lean statements and 1,506 Lean-checked proofs that pass a proof-bypass screen, with reported cost estimates.
Provides external validation through a small Mathlib upstreaming pilot: three generated lemmas were merged into Mathlib after curation, showing selected outputs can meet expert library standards.

Includes a human provability audit (138 sampled unsolved residuals, 78% proved; held-out audit of 94 statements, 84% proved) suggesting many unsolved benchmark instances are mathematically sound rather than hallucinations.
Evaluation spans multiple models and three mathematical domains, yielding useful observations about specialist vs. generalist provers, test-time compute, and model diversity.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed prompts, Algorithm 1, runtime configurations, version-pinned Lean/Mathlib settings, and released code/data.
Ethical and practical concerns are handled transparently: the authors avoid bulk submission to Mathlib, discuss review burden, and acknowledge limitations.
weaknesses: The central claim of mining 'missing' folklore lemmas is not systematically verified. There is no operational novelty/redundancy check against Mathlib beyond prompt-level instructions and the aesop triviality filter, so many of the 1,506 released proofs may restate existing facts or be semantically trivial. One of six upstreamed lemmas was rejected as redundant, underscoring this concern.

Benchmark validity is only partially established. The main audit covers 138 of 4,028 instances (3.4%) and uses a seed-stratified, open-book expert setting with AI assistance; 22% of sampled unsolved residuals were invalid. The extrapolation to an indicative ~86% solvable fraction is diagnostic rather than rigorous.

Generation-model dependence is a serious confound: GPT-5.1 is used for discovery, judging, and statement repair, and is also evaluated as a prover. The benchmark distribution and phrasing may favor GPT-5.1, even though the authors acknowledge this issue.

Main experiments do not ablate the pipeline modules or compare against simpler baselines (e.g., direct generation without Judge/Formalizer) or existing lemma-generation methods such as LeanConjecturer or Lemmanaid. Thus the contribution of modularity and the individual modules is unclear.

The Judge Module has a high false-negative rate (46% of rejected candidates were judged valid by human audit), and the Formalizer can alter statement semantics without any semantic-consistency check. These limit pipeline precision and statement fidelity.

The non-triviality filter relies solely on aesop, which is a weak proxy for semantic novelty or usefulness in downstream formalization. The benchmark's 'non-trivial' characterization is therefore not strongly supported.

The evaluation protocol uses Success@2 sequential repair and a union-of-models oracle. Main results lack standard Pass@k for the larger models, and the appendix Pass@16 result for a small specialist is not directly comparable. The 'remaining folklore gap' estimate is speculative.

Presentation and reproducibility details are incomplete: the manuscript lacks the actual repository link, Table 5 has empty PR and merge-commit fields, some references are mislabeled or incomplete, and the exact Mathlib commit is not stated in the paper.
The human audit lacks details on annotator expertise, blinding, inter-annotator agreement, and released proofs for audited instances, which weakens confidence in the reported validity rates.
